name: Capitalism
summary: Capitalism is an economic system in which most means of production are privately owned and production and prices are guided by markets, competition and the profit motive. Its defenders, Hessen and Adam Smith among them, hold that self-interested exchange under secure property rights, with a state limited to defence, justice and a few public works, produces widely shared prosperity, and they oppose tariffs, monopoly privileges and state direction of investment. The sources named leave most questions of society, culture and foreign policy open.
scope: The mainstream pro-market account of capitalism as its defining sources give it: Hessen's Concise Encyclopedia of Economics entry (economic individualism, private property, self-interest, a state that protects individual rights), Britannica's entry (private ownership of the means of production, markets, profit motive) and Adam Smith's Wealth of Nations, which both name as the founding statement of the system. It excludes the critics' account (Marx, Piketty), state capitalism, and the stricter libertarian and anarcho-capitalist wing. Questions of culture, religion, family and foreign policy lie largely outside it, so most such statements are null.

notes: Rules-7 pass. The earlier answers rested on Wikipedia and on a broad mixed-economy reading; each is now stated by Hessen, Britannica or Smith, or nulled. Themes searched in Smith (Books I-V, full text) and Hessen: trade and tariffs, colonies, interest, price controls, property, taxation, public debt, defence, justice, public works, wages, patents, labour mobility, monopoly and combination, religion, education. Smith and Hessen say nothing on social, cultural, religious, family, immigration, environmental or most constitutional questions, and Britannica gives only a definition, so those statements stay null and the uncertainty rule may exclude the ideology. Britannica's text copy was partial (paywalled), and Econlib and Britannica refused direct fetches, so the Wayback Machine copies are cited. Smith's writings on welfare, labour regulation and progressive taxation point both ways (he calls regulation in the workers' favour 'just and equitable' and a heavier tax on the rich 'not very unreasonable'), so minimum wage, unions and tax-the-wealthy stay null.
